Find your config

OpenCode Config File Location and Precedence

In OpenCode 2, use opencode.json or opencode.jsonc in the project directory. From the folder where you launch OpenCode, run opencode debug config --standalone to see which sources it reads, then opencode debug agents --standalone to inspect the resolved agent settings. In a monorepo, running from a package can load an additional config.

  1. Locate the config files
  2. Diagnose a missing file
  3. Check which file wins
  4. Check the effective agent setting
  5. Read the OpenCode 2.4.1 results

Start with opencode --version. The commands and test results here are for OpenCode 2. If you use V1, check the OpenCode migration guide for which settings carry over. Keep diagnostic output local. Configuration can contain expanded environment variables, secret file contents or private paths.

Where to put opencode.json or opencode.jsonc

Put per-project settings at the project root or in its .opencode/ folder. Put user defaults in ~/.config/opencode/ on a standard installation. Use opencode debug paths to check the actual config directory in your environment.

opencode --version
opencode debug paths
opencode debug config --standalone

In OpenCode 2.4.1, the last command returns a list of sources. A document entry identifies a file and shows the settings it contributed. A directory entry identifies a source directory. Look at the file’s own entry to confirm OpenCode read it. Run this from the folder you normally work in.

JSONC supports comments and trailing commas. Use the OpenCode configuration schema for editor validation. If you are trying to style or change the terminal interface, see the separate CLI settings for cli.json.

When a config file does not appear

  1. Check the filename and extension. The project file is opencode.json or opencode.jsonc. Check for a hidden .txt extension if you created it in a text editor.
  2. Run the source command from the same working directory as the client. In a monorepo, try from the package directory and compare the results with the repository root. Check that you opened the intended checkout or worktree.
  3. Ensure the file parses and the keys match your OpenCode version. Run the command again and check any errors. If you use Desktop or a separately running server, compare that environment as well. --standalone starts a private server for the command.

If the config contains a local model endpoint, also check the actual Ollama address and model ID.

Which OpenCode config file wins?

The official config guide describes how user defaults, repository files, nested project files and managed system settings merge. A package file can override the same setting from the repository root, and centrally managed settings can take priority over both. Unrelated settings can remain in effect.

In our OpenCode 2.4.1 test, a root opencode.jsonc overrode the same Build agent model from opencode.json. A root .opencode/opencode.json also overrode the same value when present. OPENCODE_CONFIG contributed its file and could override user defaults. The repository file still won the tested conflict. Check the current version and working directory before applying those results to a different setup.

When several files set the same value, remove the duplicate from your own config only after keeping a copy. For a managed override, check with the person who manages the installation. File precedence and permission rule order are different checks.

Verify which agent setting took effect

Run this from the same folder and look up the agent ID you actually use, such as build.

opencode debug agents --standalone

In the output, check the agent’s model object if it has an explicit agent-specific model. In this release, it contains the model ID and provider ID. The source report answers which files contributed. The agent report lets you check the final merged agent setting. If your command or session uses a separately selected model, verify that selection and endpoint where you run it.

The tests below compare an explicit agents.build.model setting. To diagnose plugin or MCP loading, use the plugin loading or MCP connection guide.
